dek_candidates: What A B Infrabuild Limited's draft red herring prospectus discloses about its two businesses, its tender-driven revenue, five years of restated numbers, and the concentration that runs through all of it.

A Mumbai infrastructure contractor that builds railway platforms and bridges, runs a ready-mix concrete plant in Thane, and draws most of its revenue from government tenders — explained from its own DRHP, page by page.
The DRHP shows a company that has been shrinking at the top line, spiking at the bottom line, and depending on a single buyer for more than half its revenue. Here is what it says.
design_notes: Explain before you cite: open each section with the plain idea, then land the filing number as proof. Do not start a paragraph with a page reference or a table row.
Every figure in the financials section is in ₹ lakhs in the filing — divide by 100 for ₹ crore and say so once, up front, so the reader is never doing arithmetic.

The five restated periods run FY2018 first and FY2014 last, anchored by the filing's own trend sentences naming FY2014, FY2015, FY2017 and FY2018 — label the table in that order and do not reorder it.
The issue price is blank throughout. Never imply a size, a valuation or a listing outcome from it; state that it is not disclosed until the price band is set.
Keep the risks section to exactly five items. Fold geographic concentration into the customer-concentration item rather than splitting it out as a sixth.
No verdict on the issue, no subscribe-or-avoid framing, no price target. The filing's numbers and disclosures carry the section; the reader draws the conclusion.

The peer comparison page is thin in the excerpts: present the disclosed ratios as disclosed, and say directly that peer identities and the issue price are not established, rather than dressing up the numbers into a table with invented labels.
One em-dash at most per 400 words of body text; prefer commas, full stops or parentheses.

beats.beat: The company describes itself as operating in two segments: creating infrastructure, and operating a ready-mix concrete plant.

Within infrastructure, the filing names three kinds of work: railways (designing and building platforms and station buildings, gauge conversion, laying track), bridges (beam, cantilever, arch, suspension, cable-stayed and truss bridges) and roadways (bituminous and concrete roads connecting highways and district roads).
The ready-mix concrete business is a single facility, described in the filing as a plant at Kashimira in Thane district, Maharashtra, which supplies concrete rather than finished structures.

Contract wins follow a fixed sequence the filing sets out: a client floats a tender, a pre-bid meeting resolves queries, the contractor bids if eligible, the job goes to the lowest quote by Letter of Acceptance, the contractor deposits a performance guarantee, and only then is the drawing issued and the site handed over.

The customer list is public bodies plus a handful of private names: Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai, Western Railway, Central Railway, Mumbai Railway Vikas Corporation, Mumbai Metropolitan Region Development Authority, Dedicated Freight Corridor Corporation of India, Sky Way Infrastructure, Dev Engineers, GCC Hotel and Krypton Corp.
Western Railway is not a new relationship — the filing says it has been a client since 2006, and that the same client accounts for 52% of the orders on hand.

Revenue concentration is disclosed at two levels: the top customers together were 57% of total revenue for the period ended March 31, 2018, and the filing separately warns that Indian Railways alone contributed 57% of revenue in Fiscal 2018.
Geographically the business is a Mumbai business that is expanding across Maharashtra, which the filing frames as a strength but which also means one city's project pipeline governs the order book.
Two operational details the filing offers as differentiators: the use of box pushing technique on projects, and a founder-led team it says has more than 20 years in the infrastructure industry.

business.heading: What A B Infrabuild actually does
business.purpose: Show the two revenue engines concretely — the construction verticals and the concrete plant — then explain the tender mechanic that decides whether the company earns anything at all, and end on how concentrated the customer base is.

beats.beat: The filing reports in ₹ lakhs, so every figure in this section is divided by 100 to reach ₹ crore — ₹6,053.05 lakhs is about ₹60.5 crore.

The restated statement of profit and loss lists five financial years with FY2018 first; the filing's own trend notes anchor the ends, showing revenue from operations falling from ₹9,021.12 lakhs in FY2015 to ₹6,053.05 lakhs in FY2018.

The full revenue series in ₹ lakhs, FY2018 back to FY2014, reads 6,053.05; 7,344.47; 7,452.76; 9,021.12; 8,661.35 — that is roughly ₹60.5 crore, ₹73.4 crore, ₹74.5 crore, ₹90.2 crore and ₹86.6 crore. The top line has shrunk over four of the five periods.

Profit before interest, depreciation and tax moves quite differently from revenue: ₹928.80 lakhs, ₹676.19 lakhs, ₹783.31 lakhs, ₹945.78 lakhs and ₹784.46 lakhs across the same five periods — so the weakest revenue year carries the second-highest operating profit.

Net profit after adjustments is the sharpest move in the filing: ₹314.66 lakhs in FY2018 against ₹15.86 lakhs in FY2017, with ₹95.95 lakhs in FY2014, ₹78.36 lakhs in FY2015 and ₹32.63 lakhs in FY2016 behind it.
Total assets in ₹ lakhs, FY2018 back to FY2014, are 8,232.15; 7,536.93; 6,295.21; 7,266.50; 7,062.34 — a balance sheet of roughly ₹82.3 crore at the latest period end.
The debt split is the important part: short-term borrowings of ₹3,537.35 lakhs (about ₹35.4 crore) dwarf long-term borrowings of ₹133.09 lakhs (about ₹1.3 crore) in FY2018.
Short-term borrowings have risen across the five periods, from ₹3,082.27 lakhs in FY2014 to ₹3,537.35 lakhs in FY2018, while long-term borrowings fell from ₹586.63 lakhs to ₹133.09 lakhs.

Two cash-related disclosures matter more than the ratios: the company states it had negative cash flow in recent financial years, and that it had ₹405.02 lakhs of unsecured loans repayable on demand as on March 31, 2018.

The filing also flags that failure to recover money from sundry debtors and trade receivables on time could affect its financial condition — which is the mechanical link between the working-capital object of the issue and the balance sheet above.

financials.heading: Five years of numbers
financials.purpose: Walk the reader through the restated statements period by period in ₹ crore, flag the top-line decline against the profit spike, and land on the balance sheet: short-term debt far larger than long-term debt, negative cash flow, and money tied up in receivables.

beats.beat: The company is controlled by one man: promoter Amit Bholanath Mishra holds 74,95,476 equity shares, or 90.949% of the pre-issue paid-up capital.
The other directors hold almost nothing by comparison — Bharat kumar Parmar, Shree Prakash Singh and Mukesh Pandey hold 300 shares each.
Key management personnel Hatim Sakerwala holds 9% of the equity shares as on the date of the draft.

The senior finance and compliance roles are held young: the chief financial officer, Anchal Pachori, is 28 and a chartered accountant, and the company secretary and compliance officer, Mohit Soni, is 26 and an associate member of the Institute of Company Secretaries of India.

Related-party dealings are small in rupees but continuous: ₹68.4 lakhs of loans taken from key management personnel or board members in FY2018, ₹57.7 lakhs of director remuneration, and ₹324.3 lakhs of outstanding payables to related parties as on March 31, 2018.
The filing states that neither the promoter nor any director has been declared a willful defaulter by the RBI, and that no criminal cases or investigations are pending against any director.
Against that, the company, its promoter and directors are currently involved in litigation pending at various stages, with no quantum or forum captured in the excerpts.

Two companies promoted by the promoter — Al-Noor Chickens Private Limited and A B Magma Automobiles Private Limited — were struck off by the Registrar of Companies in March 2016 for non-operation of business.

The filing also discloses that the company issued equity shares in the 12 months before the draft at a price which may be lower than the issue price, a point a reader comparing entry prices should know.

governance.heading: Who controls it, and the flags to read
governance.purpose: Establish promoter control as the fact that frames everything else, then set out the related-party numbers, the litigation disclosure, and the small admissions the filing makes about past conduct and past share issues.

beats.beat: The company sits in infrastructure and construction, a sector the filing defines to include power, bridges, dams, roads and urban infrastructure development.
The filing's own description of the market is unflattering in a useful way: highly fragmented, working-capital intensive, and contributing around 8% of India's GDP at constant prices.
The demand case rests on a stated investment requirement of ₹50 trillion (US$777.73 billion) in infrastructure by 2022 for sustainable development.
Named government programmes sit behind that number: the 100 Smart Cities Mission, AMRUT, Make in India and Power for All.

The filing also points to eased FDI norms across 15 sectors including real estate and construction development, and to US$24.67 billion of FDI received in construction development between April 2000 and December 2017.
Broader demand drivers it lists are rising industrialisation, urbanisation, disposable income and population growth.

Macro context the filing supplies: India's GDP growth staying above 7% in 2017, cumulative growth of 4.2% in the eight core industries in 2017-18, and infrastructure spending at 9.0% of GDP under the 12th Five-Year Plan.

On competition the filing says only that the company operates in a competitive industry with rivals in both the organised and unorganised sectors — no competitor is named anywhere in the excerpts supplied.
The headwinds the filing itself acknowledges are three: the slow pace of government projects, a working capital crunch that may affect profitability, and changes in government policy.

industry.heading: The market it sells into
industry.purpose: Give the reader the sector's shape and size as the filing tells it, name the demand drivers it lists, and be honest that the filing names no competitors — only the fact of fragmentation and three acknowledged headwinds.

beats.beat: A B Infrabuild Limited is a Mumbai-based contractor that builds railway platforms, station buildings and tracks, bridges and roads, and also runs a ready-mix concrete plant in Thane district, Maharashtra.
It earns money in two separate ways — winning construction contracts, almost entirely from government bodies, and manufacturing and selling ready-mix concrete from its own facility.
Government work is won by tender: the client floats a contract, bidders submit quotes, and the job goes to the lowest quote, with the winner then posting a performance guarantee before work starts.
The offer is 44,28,000 equity shares of ₹10 face value each, at a price the filing leaves blank, so the issue size in rupees cannot be stated from these excerpts.
Most of the money raised has one named destination: ₹1,130 lakhs (about ₹11.3 crore) for working capital, which is the cash a contractor needs to fund a project before the client pays.
The single most important fact in the filing is that Indian Railways was the largest customer at 57% of revenue in Fiscal 2018, and Western Railway alone accounted for 52% of the orders on hand.

intro.purpose: Orient a newcomer in two paragraphs: what this company physically builds, how it gets paid, what it is selling to the public, and why the customer-concentration number is the thread through the whole report.

beats.beat: The offer is 44,28,000 equity shares of ₹10 face value each, with the issue price left as a blank to be determined.

Because the price is undisclosed, the total amount the company expects to raise cannot be calculated from these excerpts — and the filing also states the issue price will be some undisclosed multiple of the ₹10 face value.

A fresh issue raises money for the company; an offer for sale sells existing shareholders' shares and the company receives nothing. The excerpts supplied here do not establish how the 44,28,000 shares split between the two, and no selling shareholder is named.
The main object of the issue is working capital: ₹1,130 lakhs, roughly ₹11.3 crore, is earmarked for it.
The second object is general corporate purposes, with the amount left blank in the filing.
The lead manager to the issue is Mark Corporate Advisors Private Limited, and the registrar is Bigshare Services Private Limited.
The filing states there is no independent agency appraising the proposed project and no monitoring agency, so deployment of the proceeds sits with management, overseen by the audit committee.

offer.heading: The issue: what is on sale, and what the money is for
offer.purpose: Lay out the offer mechanically — share count, face value, the blank issue price — name the intermediaries, list the objects, and state plainly that the excerpts do not establish a fresh-issue-versus-OFS split.

beats.beat: Customer concentration: Indian Railways alone contributed 57% of revenue in Fiscal 2018, and the filing says losing it would cause a significant dip in revenues — Western Railway separately makes up 52% of orders on hand.
Tender dependence: revenue depends on government bids being accepted, and awards go to the lowest quote, so a lost tender or a negotiated-down bid hits the order book directly.
Negative cash flow and receivables: the company had negative cash flow in recent financial years, and failure to recover trade receivables on time could affect its financial condition.

Short-term leverage: ₹3,537.35 lakhs of short-term borrowings against ₹133.09 lakhs of long-term borrowings in FY2018, plus ₹405.02 lakhs of unsecured loans repayable on demand, with a working capital crunch named in the filing's own SWOT.
Governance and geography: a 90.949% pre-issue promoter stake, continuing related-party transactions, two promoter companies struck off in 2016, and revenue concentrated in Mumbai.

risks.heading: Five risks that matter
risks.purpose: State five company-specific risks, each as a claim about this business with the filing's own numbers attached, and stop at five.

beats.beat: The filing justifies the price by comparison of accounting ratios with peer group companies, and says the issue price is determined by the company in consultation with the lead manager on that basis.
The price itself is never stated: the filing says only that the ₹10 face value carries an issue price of ₹[●] and that the issue price is [●] times the face value.

Per-share ratios are given for three years on the basis-for-issue-price pages: FY2015-16 shows 1.31, FY2016-17 shows 0.63 and FY2017-18 shows 12.59 in one table, with 4.14, 1.97 and 28.14 respectively in an adjacent set on the same page.
The peer comparison page also carries the values 12.39 and 44.71 alongside face value of ₹10 — but the excerpts supplied do not map those numbers to named companies or to labelled columns.

The honest conclusion for the reader: with the issue price undisclosed and peer names absent from the excerpts, no implied price range can be computed, and the writer should say so rather than construct one.

valuation-and-peers.heading: What the filing says about pricing
valuation-and-peers.purpose: Report exactly what is disclosed on the pricing pages, present the per-share ratios the filing does give by year, and state clearly that the issue price is blank and the peer identities are not captured — so no implied price range can be built.
